parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: acceleration as vector rate of change
hints: Hint 1: Think about what word in the definition must show that velocity can change in size or direction, and whether you need speed or velocity and change per what.
parts.proper_answer: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use velocity, not speed**
Think of acceleration as telling you how quickly motion is changing. Because velocity is a vector, a change can be a change in speed or a change in direction. So the definition must say velocity.

Step 2: **Add rate of change**
Rate of change means change per unit time, so $$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$ in words. That gives the complete definition: rate of change of velocity.

parts.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: gradient of velocity-time graph equals acceleration
hints: Hint 1: Look at the shape of Fig. 1.1 - it is a straight line through the origin, so what does its steepness represent and which two easy-to-read values at $t = 20\text{ s}$ could you use?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link gradient to acceleration**
On a velocity-time graph the gradient is $$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$ Here the line is straight, so acceleration is constant.

Step 2: **Read values and divide**
At $t = 0$, $v = 0$. At $t = 20\text{ s}$, $v = 320\text{ m s}^{-1}$. So $$a = \frac{320 - 0}{20 - 0} = 16\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: area under velocity-time graph equals displacement
hints: Hint 1: Height climbed is the distance travelled upward, so how is distance found from a velocity-time graph when you cannot just use $s = vt$ because $v$ is changing?
Hint 2: Identify the geometric shape under the line from $0$ to $20\text{ s}$ and write its area using the $20\text{ s}$ base and the $320\text{ m s}^{-1}$ top value, then convert to km.
parts.proper_answer: Distance = area under graph $= 1/2 \times 20 \times 320 = 3200\text{ m} = 3.2\text{ km}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Distance as area**
Distance travelled is the area under the velocity-time graph. Because the graph starts at zero and rises linearly, the area from $0$ to $20\text{ s}$ is a triangle.

Step 2: **Calculate triangle area**
For a triangle, $$s = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$$ $$s = \frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 320 = 3200\text{ m}$$ Divide by $1000$ to get $3.2\text{ km}$, as required.

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: The rocket gains height $\Delta h = 3200\text{ m}$ with almost constant $g$, so which energy store depends on mass, gravitational field strength and height gained?
Hint 2: Check your units: mass is $2.9 \times 10^6\text{ kg}$, $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $\Delta h$ must be in metres, not km, before multiplying.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the potential energy relation**
Gain in gravitational potential energy near Earth is $$\Delta E_P = mg\Delta h$$ where $m$ is mass, $g$ is $9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $\Delta h$ is vertical height gained.

Step 2: **Substitute in SI units**
Use $\Delta h = 3200\text{ m}$: $$\Delta E_P = (2.9 \times 10^6) \times 9.81 \times 3200$$ $$\Delta E_P \approx 9.1 \times 10^{10}\text{ J}$$ to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
key_concepts: change from rest to high speed
hints: Hint 1: The rocket starts from rest at launch and reaches about $320\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $20\text{ s}$, so which energy store starts at zero and then depends on speed squared?
Hint 2: Recall how the $1/2$, the large mass $2.9 \times 10^6\text{ kg}$ and the final speed combine, remembering to square the speed first.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the kinetic energy relation**
Gain in kinetic energy from rest is $$\Delta E_K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - 0 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ The $v^2$ is why kinetic energy grows very fast for a rocket.

Step 2: **Substitute final speed**
$$\Delta E_K = \frac{1}{2} \times (2.9 \times 10^6) \times (320)^2$$ $$\Delta E_K \approx 1.5 \times 10^{11}\text{ J}$$

parts.label: (c)(iii)
key_concepts: work done by engines equals total mechanical energy gain
average power as energy per time
hints: Hint 1: With resistive forces negligible, the engines must supply both the potential gain from (c)(i) and the kinetic gain from (c)(ii), so what is the total useful energy output in $20\text{ s}$?
Hint 2: Think how average rate of doing work relates that total energy to the $20\text{ s}$ time interval to get power in watts.
parts.proper_answer: Total work $= \Delta E_P + \Delta E_K \approx 2.4 \times 10^{11}\text{ J}$, power $= \text{work}/t \approx 1.2 \times 10^{10}\text{ W}$
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find total work done**
Neglecting resistance, work done by engines becomes mechanical energy: $$W = \Delta E_P + \Delta E_K$$ Using previous values, $W \approx 0.91 \times 10^{11} + 1.48 \times 10^{11} \approx 2.4 \times 10^{11}\text{ J}$.

Step 2: **Divide by time for average power**
Average power is $$P = \frac{W}{t}$$ $$P = \frac{2.4 \times 10^{11}}{20} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{10}\text{ W}$$ This is the average rate of energy transfer by the engines.
